cells.tense: You are open to what is coming without needing its shape first.
cells.ask: Say yes once this week before you know how it will go, and leave it at that.
cells.core:
Someone hands you something — a story, a custom, an invitation into a room you haven't stood in — and you take it without needing to know first what it will do to you. That is what's working: the door standing open while the day outside is still unknown. Going well, this looks like a person who listens to the old story and lets it land before arguing with it, who tries the unfamiliar dish, who sits with how something is done elsewhere without filing it as wrong. The group feels you taking it in, and what you take in stays yours and theirs at once. Nothing specific has arrived yet tonight, and that's fine — you're already listening rather than waiting.

Next move is small. Say yes once this week before you know how it will go, and let it be done.

cells.tense: You are feeling what is coming before it has had a chance to arrive.
cells.ask: Name one thing you already finished, and stop carrying it as unfinished.
cells.core:
You keep yourself open ahead of schedule. Something new is heading your way — or might be — and you've already felt it, priced it, decided what it will mean for the group. Readiness that's meant to be bare and unclaimed has picked up a job: bracing against a future so nothing catches you off guard. From inside it feels like sensitivity, like being tuned in early. From outside it looks like holding a door open for someone who isn't coming down the hall. The group reads your anticipation as pressure and starts performing for you instead of sharing with you.

What works is finishing something already in hand. Name one thing that's done this week, bare, and hand it over as complete.

cells.tense: You were open once, and something shut before you could take anything in.
cells.ask: Take one custom you know by heart and do it this week as if you'd never seen it.
cells.core:
Things that should reach you — a piece of the tradition, a person's story, something worth carrying — arrive and stop short. You stand in rooms where meaning gets passed around, and you're not taking any of it in, and after enough of that the whole thing goes flat and you call the tradition empty. The value is still there in what's being handed to you. What's gone is the taking of it. You keep standing at the edge of the circle, close enough to hear, not close enough to be changed by what's being said in it.

The way back is fresh attention, not effort. Take one practice you know by heart and do it as if you'd never seen it — same act, new eyes.

cells.tense: You are already taking things in, and you call it just being agreeable.
cells.ask: Catch one thing that comes back to you this week and say out loud that it did.
cells.core:
Someone tells you how their family does it, someone passes on a story, someone shows you the way a thing is made here — and you take it in. It changes how you move afterward, which is what receiving is for. Going well, this looks like a person who says where something came from when they use it later, who gives the recipe credit, who lets the old way show through their own hands. But you describe all of that as simply going along, being easy, not objecting. The taking-in stays invisible to you, and the exchange stays one-sided, because you don't say what arrived.

Say where one of those things landed, once, in front of the person who gave it.

attempts.check: The record shows the medicine cards (Allure, Achievement, Realization, Reciprocity) but says nothing about the person's history, so no cell may claim what happened behind a closed door or who was there. A reader could reasonably object that 'open to what's new' describes everyone in a shared tradition, so the bend is what must carry each cell, not the capacity. The asks survive a wrong read because each is one visible act — saying yes once, naming a finished thing, touching a custom fresh, watching one exchange — useful whether or not the diagnosis lands. The sentence that serves me too well is any line about the heart opening; it flatters the card and tells the person nothing they can use.

attempts.check: The record gives the mechanism and the medicine but not one biographical fact about the person, so nothing here may say what happened behind a closed door, who was in that room, or how long ago. A reader could fairly object that 'open to what's new' sounds like every person in a shared tradition, so each cell has to lean on the bend, not the bare capacity. Each ask stays useful even if my read is wrong, because each one is a single act someone could do today with nothing in hand — one yes, one finished thing named, one practice touched fresh, one exchange noticed and said out loud. The line that serves me rather than them is any quiet praise of openness itself; it sounds wise and describes no moment they'd recognise.
